script.opening: (Nasal voice, tissues nearby, friendly.) "Every spring it's the same — I'm sneezing constantly, my nose runs like a tap, it's blocked at night, and my eyes itch. I take a hay-fever tablet but honestly it's barely touching it this year, and I'm shattered at work. Can I have something stronger? Maybe some steroids or a stronger antihistamine?"

facts.text: Sneezing, runny clear nose, blocked at night, itchy nose and itchy watery eyes. "Both sides, always. Spring into early summer, every year" — since her teens. Worse on high-pollen days and after being outside.
If asked: "No, nothing like that" — no one-sided blockage, no blood from the nose, no crusting, no facial pain, numbness or swelling, no loss of smell, no hearing change, no double vision.
"I wake up blocked, so I sleep badly, and I'm foggy in lessons. Sneezing in front of thirty children isn't great either."

"Whatever the pharmacy gives me — I'd have to check the box" (it's chlorphenamine). "Only when it's bad, really." Has tried a nasal spray: "Not regularly, no. Just the tablets when it's bad." Used a steroid spray once for a few days and stopped because it "didn't do anything".
If asked: "Not that I know of" — no wheeze or night cough. Eczema as a child. No allergies to medicines.
No regular medicines. On the combined pill. Not pregnant or breastfeeding.
Primary school teacher, married, no pets, non-smoker. Walks to school past a park. Sleeps with the window open.

Pleasant, a bit tired. If asked what she was hoping for: "I've heard there's an injection that sorts you out for the whole summer. Or just a stronger tablet." If asked about worries: "Being useless at work. I can't take time off for hay fever, and I feel like I'm letting the kids down." Curious and engaged when the spray technique is explained: "What's the right way, then?" If given the steroid injection without discussion, accept (the trap).

ice.ideas: "The tablet's stopped working — I need something stronger, or that steroid injection."
ice.concerns: Sleep and concentration at work; letting her class down; frustration that the usual remedy isn't working.
ice.expectations: "A stronger tablet — or the injection that lasts all summer."

cues: "Only when it's bad, really." — as-needed use; invites the under-treatment discussion.
"I'm foggy in lessons." — impact on work and sleep.
"An injection that sorts you out for the whole summer." — expectation to address.

checkpoints.text: Confirms seasonal ALLERGIC RHINITIS from the bilateral, seasonal, itch/sneeze/rhinorrhoea + itchy-eyes picture, and assesses triggers, impact (sleep/work) and atopy — noting the bilateral/seasonal nature is reassuring
Identifies UNDER-TREATMENT (PRN oral antihistamine alone) as the likely reason for "failure" — not a need for something exotic

Makes a REGULAR intranasal CORTICOSTEROID the mainstay (daily through the season, BSACI 2017; starting a little before the season is common practice) and counsels correct SPRAY TECHNIQUE (head forward, opposite hand, aim away from septum, gentle sniff, days-to-weeks for effect)

Lays out the full LADDER and add-ons — avoidance, non-sedating antihistamine, intranasal antihistamine/combination spray, antihistamine eye drops, saline; leukotriene antagonist in selected cases only, with the MHRA montelukast neuropsychiatric warnings (September 2019; April 2024); short oral steroid only for severe acute flares (not depot); ENT/allergy referral for immunotherapy in refractory cases — and avoids long-term decongestant sprays

EXPLICITLY voices the rhinitis RED FLAGS that are not simple hay fever (persistent unilateral obstruction, unilateral bloody discharge, unilateral mass, facial pain/numbness, orbital symptoms) and that they warrant ENT referral on clinical grounds — while correctly reassuring that her bilateral seasonal picture does not fit them
Acknowledges the real impact on sleep/concentration/work and the frustration, and frames the plan as getting control rather than dismissing her request
Explains why regular treatment and technique matter (rather than just "a stronger pill"), checking understanding and supporting adherence

Safety-nets and follows up: realistic timeframe for the intranasal steroid to work, a flare plan, when to return or be referred (including the unilateral/bloody red flags), and review of control — the proper ladder with safety-netting, not just a stronger antihistamine

worked.txt: "This is classic hay fever — seasonal, both sides, itchy sneezy nose and eyes. The fact it’s both sides and comes each spring is actually reassuring; it’s allergy, not something sinister."

"Here’s why I think it’s ‘stopped working’: a tablet now and then isn’t really enough for symptoms this bad. The treatment that does the heavy lifting is a steroid nose spray used EVERY day through the season — not just when you’re bad — and it’s worth starting it a little before the pollen usually kicks off for you, so it’s already working."

"Technique is half the battle. Shake it, tip your head slightly forward, use your opposite hand and aim the spray towards the outer wall of your nostril, away from the middle — then a gentle sniff, not a hard snort. Done at the septum or snorted hard, it gives nosebleeds and doesn’t work. Give it up to a couple of weeks."

"So: regular steroid spray plus a daily non-drowsy antihistamine, antihistamine drops for your eyes, and saline rinses. Avoidance helps too — windows shut on high-pollen days, wraparound sunglasses, shower and change after you’ve been out. If a spell is really severe — say around exams — we can use a short oral steroid course, and if it’s ever unmanageable year after year, there’s referral for allergy treatment."

"One important thing to know for the future: hay fever is both sides. If you ever get a blocked nose on just ONE side that won’t clear, one-sided bleeding or blood-stained discharge, or facial pain or numbness, that’s different — come back, because that needs an ENT check. That’s not what you’ve got now, but worth knowing."

"Give the spray a fortnight of regular use and let’s review how you’re sleeping and coping at work. If it’s still not controlled despite good technique, we’ll step up. And those one-sided warning signs — don’t sit on them."

f.learning: Seasonal sneezing with bilateral nasal itch, watery rhinorrhoea, congestion and itchy watery eyes is classic ALLERGIC RHINITIS (hay fever), and the bilateral, symmetrical, seasonal pattern is itself reassuring. The commonest reason it "stops working" is UNDER-TREATMENT: a PRN oral antihistamine alone is insufficient for moderate-to-severe disease, where the mainstay is a REGULAR intranasal corticosteroid used DAILY through the season (BSACI 2017; starting a little before the season is common practice rather than a guideline figure), and most apparent failure reflects irregular use and poor SPRAY TECHNIQUE rather than a need for something exotic — so counsel technique explicitly (head slightly forward, opposite hand, aim away from the septum toward the outer wall, gentle sniff, days-to-2-weeks for effect). The full ladder: allergen avoidance; regular intranasal steroid + a non-sedating antihistamine; add intranasal antihistamine/combination spray, antihistamine eye drops and saline; consider a leukotriene antagonist selectively (especially with asthma), counselling on the montelukast neuropsychiatric warnings (MHRA Drug Safety Update September 2019; April 2024), and a SHORT oral steroid course only for severe acute flares (never depot injections); and ENT/allergy referral for immunotherapy in severe, refractory, single-allergen cases — while avoiding prolonged decongestant sprays (rhinitis medicamentosa). Crucially, voice the rhinitis RED FLAGS that are NOT simple hay fever and warrant ENT referral: persistent UNILATERAL nasal obstruction, unilateral blood-stained/bloody discharge, a unilateral mass/polyp, facial pain/swelling/numbness, or orbital symptoms — which can indicate a sinonasal tumour (BSACI 2017). ENT referral for unilateral or bloody features is made on clinical grounds, with urgency set by the features, and this red-flag teaching must be made explicit as safety-netting.

knowledge.guideline: BSACI guideline for the diagnosis and management of allergic and non-allergic rhinitis (Scadding et al., 2017) · ARIA-EAACI (international, 2024–2025) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2019; April 2024) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Spring-time, two-sided sneezing, itch, running and blocked nose with itchy eyes is seasonal allergic rhinitis. When an as-needed tablet stops working, the usual problem is under-treatment: a regular intranasal steroid with good technique is the mainstay.

points.t: Bilateral sneezing, itch, watery discharge and blockage with itchy eyes in the pollen season is allergic rhinitis. Ask about impact on sleep, work and concentration, and about asthma, which often coexists with rhinitis (BSACI 2017).

BSACI 2017: an intranasal corticosteroid is the treatment of choice for moderate to severe allergic rhinitis, used regularly through the season, not as needed. It takes days to work fully. Fluticasone or mometasone: 2 sprays into each nostril once daily in adults (SPC).
Head tilted slightly forward, spray with the opposite hand aimed away from the septum towards the outer wall, sniff gently. Poor technique causes nosebleeds, crusting and apparent treatment failure.

Allergen avoidance → regular intranasal steroid plus a non-sedating antihistamine (for example cetirizine or loratadine 10 mg once daily) → a combination intranasal steroid and antihistamine spray (BSACI 2017 second line), antihistamine eye drops, saline rinses. Oral prednisolone only as a short rescue course for severe symptoms at key times (dose per BNF); BSACI 2017 does not recommend depot steroid injections. Specialist referral for immunotherapy if uncontrolled despite optimal treatment.

Sedating antihistamines impair driving and performance. Decongestant sprays such as xylometazoline: no more than 5 consecutive days (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2026) because of rebound congestion. Montelukast carries neuropsychiatric warnings (MHRA Drug Safety Update September 2019; April 2024) and ARIA-EAACI (international) does not favour it over an oral antihistamine.

Persistent one-sided blockage, one-sided bloody discharge, facial pain, swelling or numbness, or eye symptoms such as double vision point to other pathology, including sinonasal tumours, and need ENT assessment (BSACI 2017). NICE suspected-cancer guidance has no sinonasal criterion, so refer on clinical grounds with urgency set by the features.

Explicit one-sided red flags; review in about four weeks; step-up plan; teach-back on technique.

Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

model.text: Hello Mrs Soneji, I’m Dr Lee. Can you hear and see me okay? … Great. What’s been happening?
model.why: Open question after checking the video link

model.text: Every spring it’s the same — sneezing constantly, my nose runs like a tap, it’s blocked at night, and my eyes itch. I take a hay-fever tablet but it’s barely touching it this year, and I’m shattered at work. Can I have something stronger? Maybe steroids?

That sounds exhausting, especially in a classroom. I’d like to understand exactly how it’s affecting you and what you’re using now, then we’ll build a plan that actually gets on top of it. Does that sound okay?
model.why: Validates and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
Is it both sides of your nose equally, and does it come every year at the same time?
Both sides, always. Spring into early summer, every year.
Have you ever had blockage on just one side that doesn’t clear, bleeding or blood-stained mucus from one side, or pain or numbness in your face?
No, nothing like that.
How is it affecting your sleep and your work?
I wake up blocked, so I sleep badly, and I’m foggy in lessons. Sneezing in front of thirty children isn’t great either.
Which tablet do you take, and how often?
Whatever the pharmacy gives me — I’d have to check the box. Only when it’s bad, really.
And have you ever used a steroid nose spray every day through the season?
Not regularly, no. Just the tablets when it’s bad.
That’s really helpful. Do you have asthma or wheeze, especially in the pollen season?
Not that I know of.
You asked about steroids. What were you picturing?
model.why: Explores her idea behind the request

model.text: I’ve heard there’s an injection that sorts you out for the whole summer. Or just a stronger tablet.
What worries you most about this season?
Being useless at work. I can’t take time off for hay fever, and I feel like I’m letting the kids down.

Here’s my thinking. This is classic hay fever — both sides, every spring, itchy nose and eyes. That pattern is reassuring; it’s allergy, not something more serious. And I think the reason it’s “stopped working” is that a tablet now and then isn’t enough for symptoms this strong.
model.why: Working diagnosis plus the under-treatment insight

model.text: So a stronger tablet won’t help?

Not much. The treatment that does the heavy lifting is a steroid nose spray used every day through the season — not just on bad days. It works in the lining of the nose, where the problem is — but only if it’s used properly, so let me show you how.
What’s the right way, then?

Tip your head slightly forward, not back. Use your right hand for the left nostril and the other way round, and aim towards the outer side, away from the middle. Then a gentle sniff, not a big snort. Give it up to a couple of weeks to work fully.
I’d never have guessed the direction mattered.

So my suggestion: the steroid spray every day, a non-drowsy antihistamine tablet every day in the season, antihistamine eye drops, and a saline rinse if you like. On high-pollen days, windows shut, wraparound sunglasses, and a shower and change when you get in. How does that sound?
model.why: Shares the ladder and checks acceptability

model.text: Doable. What about the injection I’d heard about?

I understand why it’s appealing. The steroid injection affects the whole body for weeks, with risks such as thinning bones and raised sugar, and specialists don’t recommend it for hay fever. If a really bad spell ever coincides with something crucial, a short course of steroid tablets is safer. And if it’s still uncontrolled despite all this, there’s specialist allergy treatment called immunotherapy.
model.why: Declines depot steroid with reasons and outlines next steps

model.text: Fair enough. I’d rather do it properly.

One thing for the future: hay fever affects both sides. If you ever get blockage on one side that won’t clear, one-sided bleeding or bloody mucus, or pain or numbness in your face, come back — that needs an ear, nose and throat check. That’s not what you have now.
Okay. Good to know.
Could you tell me back how you’ll use the spray, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Every day, head forward, opposite hand, aim to the outside, gentle sniff. Give it two weeks. Tablet every day, drops for my eyes.
Perfect. Let’s speak again in about four weeks to see how you’re sleeping and managing at work. If it’s still not controlled, we’ll step up. Anything else?
No, that’s great. Thank you.

social.t: Poor sleep and daytime fog affect teaching. Hay fever can also affect people sitting exams; the same principles apply to the children she teaches.
Many hay-fever products are available from community pharmacies; discuss prescription versus over-the-counter supply.

legal.t: Sedating antihistamines impair driving; it is an offence to drive when impaired by drugs, including medicines (Road Traffic Act 1988). Prefer non-sedating options.

professional.t: NHS England (2018) guidance advises that mild to moderate hay fever treatment should not routinely be prescribed in primary care; explain local policy transparently and where she can buy the recommended products.
Declining a depot steroid injection is a shared decision: explain the risks and the better alternatives rather than just saying no (GMC decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on sprays and technique; the Met Office pollen forecast helps plan avoidance; Allergy UK has patient information.

redFlags: Facial pain, swelling or numbness; double vision or bulging eye
psychosocial: Impact on sleep, concentration and teaching
Pressure not to take time off
As-needed use of treatment; no regular nasal spray
ice: Idea: “I need a stronger tablet or a steroid injection”
Concern: being useless at work this season

playbook.diagnosis: Seasonal allergic rhinitis with conjunctivitis, moderate to severe given the impact on sleep and work, under-treated with as-needed oral antihistamine alone. The bilateral, seasonal pattern and absence of one-sided features are reassuring.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This is hay fever — your nose and eyes overreacting to pollen. Both sides, every spring: that’s reassuring. A tablet now and then damps down only part of it; the daily nose spray calms the inflammation where it starts.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted something stronger because you can’t afford to be foggy in front of your class. I think we can get you there — just with a better-used treatment rather than a bigger one.”
management.psychosocial: Tie the plan to sleeping through the night and clear mornings at work; make the spray work first time by teaching technique.
sharedPlan: Daily intranasal steroid through the season with technique taught (BSACI 2017)
Daily non-sedating antihistamine, antihistamine eye drops, saline; pollen avoidance
No depot steroid; short oral steroid rescue only for severe key times; immunotherapy referral if uncontrolled despite optimal treatment
safetyNet: One-sided blockage, bloody discharge, facial pain or numbness, eye symptoms — return for ENT assessment
Review in about four weeks; step up if still uncontrolled

pitfalls.intro: This looks like an easy station, which is why it is failed: candidates prescribe and close. The marks are in finding out why treatment failed, teaching the spray, and voicing what is not hay fever.

items.fail: Swapping one antihistamine for another and ending the consultation.
items.why: “Management not in line with current UK best practice.” BSACI 2017 makes the intranasal steroid the treatment of choice for moderate to severe disease.
items.fix: “The spray, every day, is what does the heavy lifting.”

items.fail: Prescribing a steroid spray without teaching technique.
items.why: Poor technique causes nosebleeds and apparent failure, and the spray is then abandoned.
items.fix: Teach the technique, then check it with teach-back.

items.fail: Agreeing to a depot steroid injection because she asks for it.
items.why: BSACI 2017 does not recommend depot steroid for rhinitis because of its adverse risk–benefit profile.
items.fix: Explain the whole-body effects and offer the better alternatives, including a short rescue course if ever needed.

items.why: Red-flag safety-netting is a marked item even when the diagnosis is benign.
items.fix: “If it’s ever just one side, or there’s bleeding or facial numbness, come back.”

items.fail: Treating the request for “something stronger” as the agenda and never asking what she pictured.
items.why: “Did not explore the patient’s ideas.” The injection she has heard about is the key to shared decision-making here.
items.fix: “What were you picturing?” Then respond to it directly.

items.fail: No review plan, so she stops the spray again after a week.
items.why: Follow-up that sets expectations is part of safe management.
items.fix: Explain it takes up to two weeks, and book a review in about four weeks.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uncovers the as-needed pattern; teaches technique and checks it with teach-back; handles the injection request with reasons; voices the one-sided red flags explicitly; links the plan to her work and sleep.

avoid.why: Escalating the tablet misses the under-treatment and the mainstay therapy.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Spring-time, two-sided sneezing, itch, running and blocked nose with itchy eyes is seasonal allergic rhinitis. When an as-needed tablet stops working, the usual problem is under-treatment: a regular intranasal steroid with good technique is the mainstay.

points.t: Bilateral sneezing, itch, watery discharge and blockage with itchy eyes in the pollen season is allergic rhinitis. Ask about impact on sleep, work and concentration, and about asthma, which often coexists with rhinitis (BSACI 2017).

BSACI 2017: an intranasal corticosteroid is the treatment of choice for moderate to severe allergic rhinitis, used regularly through the season, not as needed. It takes days to work fully. Fluticasone or mometasone: 2 sprays into each nostril once daily in adults (SPC).
Head tilted slightly forward, spray with the opposite hand aimed away from the septum towards the outer wall, sniff gently. Poor technique causes nosebleeds, crusting and apparent treatment failure.

Allergen avoidance → regular intranasal steroid plus a non-sedating antihistamine (for example cetirizine or loratadine 10 mg once daily) → a combination intranasal steroid and antihistamine spray (BSACI 2017 second line), antihistamine eye drops, saline rinses. Oral prednisolone only as a short rescue course for severe symptoms at key times (dose per BNF); BSACI 2017 does not recommend depot steroid injections. Specialist referral for immunotherapy if uncontrolled despite optimal treatment.

Sedating antihistamines impair driving and performance. Decongestant sprays such as xylometazoline: no more than 5 consecutive days (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2026) because of rebound congestion. Montelukast carries neuropsychiatric warnings (MHRA Drug Safety Update September 2019; April 2024) and ARIA-EAACI (international) does not favour it over an oral antihistamine.

Persistent one-sided blockage, one-sided bloody discharge, facial pain, swelling or numbness, or eye symptoms such as double vision point to other pathology, including sinonasal tumours, and need ENT assessment (BSACI 2017). NICE suspected-cancer guidance has no sinonasal criterion, so refer on clinical grounds with urgency set by the features.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her describe the symptoms and the impact before discussing treatment.
Teaching, sleep, concentration, pressure not to take time off, and feelings of letting the children down.
Picked up “only when it’s bad” and the injection she had heard about as cues, and explored both.
Idea (a stronger tablet or a steroid injection); concern (coping at work); expectation (something stronger today).
Clinical diagnosis from the history; no tests needed for classic seasonal disease; asked about asthma.
Allergic rhinitis vs non-allergic rhinitis, decongestant overuse, nasal polyps and one-sided pathology.
Screened one-sided blockage, bloody discharge, facial pain or numbness; knew NICE suspected-cancer guidance has no sinonasal criterion.
Seasonal allergic rhinitis under-treated by as-needed oral antihistamine alone.
Regular intranasal steroid with taught technique, daily non-sedating antihistamine, eye drops, saline, avoidance (BSACI 2017).
Asthma asked about; depot steroid declined with reasons; decongestant and montelukast cautions; immunotherapy route.
Explicit one-sided red flags; review in about four weeks; step-up plan; teach-back on technique.

social.t: Poor sleep and daytime fog affect teaching. Hay fever can also affect people sitting exams; the same principles apply to the children she teaches.
Many hay-fever products are available from community pharmacies; discuss prescription versus over-the-counter supply.

legal.t: Sedating antihistamines impair driving; it is an offence to drive when impaired by drugs, including medicines (Road Traffic Act 1988). Prefer non-sedating options.

professional.t: NHS England (2018) guidance advises that mild to moderate hay fever treatment should not routinely be prescribed in primary care; explain local policy transparently and where she can buy the recommended products.
Declining a depot steroid injection is a shared decision: explain the risks and the better alternatives rather than just saying no (GMC decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on sprays and technique; the Met Office pollen forecast helps plan avoidance; Allergy UK has patient information.

redFlags: Facial pain, swelling or numbness; double vision or bulging eye
psychosocial: Impact on sleep, concentration and teaching
Pressure not to take time off
As-needed use of treatment; no regular nasal spray
ice: Idea: “I need a stronger tablet or a steroid injection”
Concern: being useless at work this season

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Seasonal allergic rhinitis with conjunctivitis, moderate to severe given the impact on sleep and work, under-treated with as-needed oral antihistamine alone. The bilateral, seasonal pattern and absence of one-sided features are reassuring.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “This is hay fever — your nose and eyes overreacting to pollen. Both sides, every spring: that’s reassuring. A tablet now and then damps down only part of it; the daily nose spray calms the inflammation where it starts.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted something stronger because you can’t afford to be foggy in front of your class. I think we can get you there — just with a better-used treatment rather than a bigger one.”
management.psychosocial: Tie the plan to sleeping through the night and clear mornings at work; make the spray work first time by teaching technique.
sharedPlan: Daily intranasal steroid through the season with technique taught (BSACI 2017)
Daily non-sedating antihistamine, antihistamine eye drops, saline; pollen avoidance
No depot steroid; short oral steroid rescue only for severe key times; immunotherapy referral if uncontrolled despite optimal treatment
safetyNet: One-sided blockage, bloody discharge, facial pain or numbness, eye symptoms — return for ENT assessment
Review in about four weeks; step up if still uncontrolled

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This looks like an easy station, which is why it is failed: candidates prescribe and close. The marks are in finding out why treatment failed, teaching the spray, and voicing what is not hay fever.

items.fail: Swapping one antihistamine for another and ending the consultation.
items.why: “Management not in line with current UK best practice.” BSACI 2017 makes the intranasal steroid the treatment of choice for moderate to severe disease.
items.fix: “The spray, every day, is what does the heavy lifting.”

items.fail: Prescribing a steroid spray without teaching technique.
items.why: Poor technique causes nosebleeds and apparent failure, and the spray is then abandoned.
items.fix: Teach the technique, then check it with teach-back.

items.fail: Agreeing to a depot steroid injection because she asks for it.
items.why: BSACI 2017 does not recommend depot steroid for rhinitis because of its adverse risk–benefit profile.
items.fix: Explain the whole-body effects and offer the better alternatives, including a short rescue course if ever needed.

items.why: Red-flag safety-netting is a marked item even when the diagnosis is benign.
items.fix: “If it’s ever just one side, or there’s bleeding or facial numbness, come back.”

items.fail: Treating the request for “something stronger” as the agenda and never asking what she pictured.
items.why: “Did not explore the patient’s ideas.” The injection she has heard about is the key to shared decision-making here.
items.fix: “What were you picturing?” Then respond to it directly.

items.fail: No review plan, so she stops the spray again after a week.
items.why: Follow-up that sets expectations is part of safe management.
items.fix: Explain it takes up to two weeks, and book a review in about four weeks.
